paragraphs: This paper presents an algorithm and software package for fitting sparse generalized linear models. Sparsity means that a model can use only a subset of the available features, with a penalty encouraging unnecessary coefficients to disappear. The work extends beyond the familiar L1 penalty to support both convex and non-convex penalties, provided they are separable across coefficients.

The algorithm combines coordinate descent, working sets, and Anderson acceleration. These components organize optimization around individual coefficients, selected groups of variables, and accelerated progress between iterations. Their combination is intended to make a broad family of sparse modeling problems practical, rather than requiring a separate specialized solver for every choice of fitting objective and penalty.

The authors report solving problems involving millions of samples and features in seconds and show improvements over existing algorithms across extensive evaluations. They also report handling models previously unsupported by available approaches. The accompanying skglm package makes the method accessible through a scikit-learn-compatible interface and allows customized data-fitting terms and penalties, connecting the optimization contribution to flexible model development.
neurips-2022-beyond-l1-faster-and-better.tldr: skglm combines accelerated optimization with flexible software to fit large sparse models using convex or non-convex separable penalties.

paragraphs: Breaking Bad introduces a dataset for studying how to reconstruct objects from broken fragments. It contains more than one million fractured objects generated from ten thousand original models. A physically based simulation produces different ways each object can break, giving researchers a large collection of reassembly problems with varied fragment geometry.

The central distinction is between assembling meaningful components and reassembling damage. Existing datasets often divide objects into recognizable parts that reflect how an object is constructed. Breaking Bad instead represents destruction: the pieces arise from fracture rather than from semantic categories. Consequently, understanding what an object is does not by itself specify how its fragments should fit together.

The authors characterize the dataset using several geometric measurements and evaluate three leading deep learning methods for shape assembly under multiple settings. Their experiments show that the dataset presents substantial difficulty for these methods. The contribution is therefore both a benchmark and evidence that fractured-object reassembly deserves model designs specifically suited to geometric fragments.
neurips-2022-breaking-bad-a-dataset-for-.tldr: Breaking Bad provides over one million simulated fractured objects to benchmark the difficult task of reconstructing shapes from fragments.

paragraphs: This paper introduces combinatorial music generation, a task for creating varied background music that fits requested conditions. The approach generates short musical samples with descriptive metadata and combines those samples into complete music. This organization connects control over individual musical pieces with the broader goal of producing music suited to a particular context.

To support the task, the authors introduce ComMU, a symbolic music dataset containing short samples and twelve associated musical metadata fields. Professional composers manually construct the dataset using an objective guideline intended to encourage regularity. The metadata also captures aspects of composers’ intentions, giving generation systems information about how samples are meant to function musically.

The reported results show that metadata alone can guide the generation of diverse, high-quality music. The authors also find that particular metadata, including track role and extended chord quality, improves automatic composition capability. These findings support the usefulness of musically informative conditioning: the dataset supplies both composable material and structured descriptions that help direct its generation.
neurips-2022-commu-dataset-for-combinato.tldr: ComMU pairs composer-created musical samples with twelve metadata fields to support controllable generation and combination of background music.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to compress tensor-structured data using random projections that themselves have tensor-network structure. Such compression can accelerate tensor decomposition and kernel regression. Earlier constructions targeted particular input structures; the authors develop a systematic approach using Gaussian random tensors for more general networks, aiming to keep both the compressed representation and the computation small.

The analysis covers embeddings that can be expressed as a sequence of sketching matrices. It supplies a sufficient condition for controlling accuracy and derives computational lower bounds for embeddings satisfying that condition whose sketch size is smaller than every input dimension. The resulting algorithm uses a sketch size that grows linearly with the number of input dimensions being sketched.

The efficiency guarantees depend on explicit conditions. With classical dense matrix multiplication for tensor contractions, the algorithm comes within an O(sqrt(m)) factor of the derived lower bound, where m is sketch size. When every input tensor has a dimension requiring sketching, its asymptotic cost is optimal within the analyzed setting. Applications include faster CP decomposition in multiple regimes and an optimality result for an existing tensor-train rounding algorithm.
neurips-2022-cost-efficient-gaussian-ten.tldr: Gaussian tensor-network sketches compress broadly structured tensor inputs with accuracy conditions and computational guarantees, including optimal cost in a specified setting.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns from a fixed dataset, making unsupported actions a concern: their values can be mistakenly overestimated. Adversarial methods can encourage a learned policy to remain close to the recorded behavior. However, asking one generator both to reproduce the data distribution and to maximize return can create conflicting objectives, especially when the data contains suboptimal behavior.

DASCO divides these responsibilities between two generators. One seeks high returns, while the other captures the remaining parts of the dataset’s distribution. Their mixture is trained to stay close to the behavior policy. This lets the return-seeking generator concentrate on useful behavior without requiring that generator alone to reproduce every kind of action in the dataset.

The authors show that this arrangement approximates a support constraint: the policy can focus on high-performing behavior supported by the data rather than matching the entire distribution. On benchmark tasks requiring learning from suboptimal data, DASCO significantly outperforms earlier methods imposing distribution constraints. The result supports separating distribution coverage from the objective of finding a strong policy.
neurips-2022-dasco-dual-generator-advers.tldr: DASCO uses two adversarial generators to pursue high-return behavior while their mixture remains close to the offline data distribution.

paragraphs: Action recognition systems can rely heavily on the setting of a video instead of the person’s movement. That background bias is difficult to measure with conventional evaluation because a correct action label does not reveal which visual evidence drove the prediction. This paper introduces the Human-centric Analysis Toolkit, or HAT, to examine that dependence more directly.

HAT automatically creates manipulated videos using image segmentation and video inpainting. These synthetic changes provide a way to evaluate learned background bias without collecting new manual video annotations. The contribution is an evaluation tool: it makes it possible to investigate what existing recognition models attend to, beyond whether they predict the right category on ordinary videos.

The authors use HAT to analyze 74 models trained on Kinetics and find that all examined models focus more on background scenery than human motion. They also report that training with fewer frames and using dense rather than uniform temporal sampling appear to worsen the bias. These findings identify evaluation concerns and design choices worth investigating when building more generalizable action recognizers.
neurips-2022-enabling-detailed-action-re.tldr: HAT automatically manipulates videos to measure background bias, finding strong scene dependence across 74 evaluated action recognition models.

paragraphs: An agent working with a person may need to balance task performance with behavior that the person expects. Those expectations can differ from the agent’s optimal strategy because the person has an incomplete or inaccurate understanding of the task. Explicable Policy Search, or EPS, addresses this problem in reinforcement learning with stochastic dynamics and continuous states and actions.

The challenge is that human expectations are hidden. Directly asking someone to specify their beliefs about environmental dynamics and rewards is impractical. The authors show that the information needed for EPS can be encoded necessarily and sufficiently in a surrogate reward function, which can be learned from human feedback on the agent’s behavior. That surrogate then reshapes the agent’s reward.

The paper establishes an equivalence between this reward reshaping and searching for an explicable policy. Evaluations use navigation domains with synthetic human models and an autonomous-driving domain with a user study. The results suggest that EPS can reconcile performance with human expectations, providing evidence for its relevance to human-agent teamwork rather than assuming that task reward alone captures successful collaboration.
neurips-2022-explicable-policy-search-5f.tldr: EPS learns a surrogate reward from human feedback to balance task performance with expected behavior in continuous, stochastic environments.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether representations learned by protein language models are useful for predicting protein function. Its particular focus is Evoformer, the component trained within AlphaFold for structure prediction. The motivating question is whether a representation developed for structural reasoning also contains information that can support a different kind of biological prediction.

The empirical comparison covers three models with different relationships to protein information: ESM-1b operates on single sequences, MSA-Transformer uses multiple sequence alignments, and Evoformer is associated with structural prediction. The study asks whether Evoformer’s representations support function prediction and, if so, whether they could replace the other two models. It also examines dependence on evolution-related protein data.

A further question is whether the models provide complementary information, which matters when deciding whether one representation can stand in for another. The abstract describes the comparative study and its questions but does not state which model wins or whether replacement is justified. Its supported contribution is the empirical examination of these representation choices, with code and datasets made available for reproducibility.
neurips-2022-exploring-evolution-aware-f.tldr: The paper compares three protein language models to investigate Evoformer’s usefulness for function prediction and the models’ dependence on evolutionary information.

paragraphs: Small decision trees provide understandable predictions, but finding the best tree of a given size while satisfying fairness requirements can be computationally expensive. This paper develops a faster approach using dynamic programming. The attraction is that trees naturally split into smaller problems, allowing optimization to exploit their structure.

A global fairness constraint complicates that decomposition because choices in one part of the tree can affect whether the entire tree is fair. The authors address this dependence by maintaining upper and lower bounds on the final fairness values that partial solutions could achieve. Those bounds allow candidate solutions to be compared and pruned before a complete tree has been built.

The reported results show fair, optimal trees being found several orders of magnitude faster than with previous methods, including on larger datasets that had been out of reach. The speedup also enables computation of the full accuracy-fairness Pareto front: the set of trade-offs where improving one objective requires sacrificing the other. This makes the method useful for examining choices among competing fairness and accuracy targets.
neurips-2022-fair-and-optimal-decision-t.tldr: Fairness bounds make dynamic programming practical for finding optimal decision trees and mapping accuracy-fairness trade-offs much faster.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets clients train a shared model without pooling their data. Good performance on participating clients, however, does not necessarily mean the model will work well for a new client. FedSR addresses this domain-generalization problem while preserving the decentralized setting, where methods requiring shared data across domains cannot be applied directly.

The approach encourages the model to learn a simple representation containing information essential for prediction. It combines an L2 penalty on the representation with a conditional mutual-information penalty between the representation and the input, given the label. The latter discourages retaining input details beyond what the label requires, aiming to reduce reliance on spurious cues such as backgrounds.

The authors connect these two objectives theoretically to representation alignment, a central idea in domain generalization. Their experiments suggest substantial improvements over relevant baselines for generalizing federated models to unknown target data. The significance is that generalization is addressed through the learned representation while respecting the data-sharing restrictions that define this federated setting.
neurips-2022-fedsr-a-simple-and-effectiv.tldr: FedSR encourages simple, label-relevant representations to improve federated models’ generalization to unseen clients without sharing client data.

paragraphs: Geoclidean studies whether vision models can recognize geometric concepts after seeing only a few examples. Humans readily reason about ideal lines and circles even though perfect geometric primitives are uncommon in natural scenes. The paper asks whether models pretrained on natural images acquire a comparable sensitivity to Euclidean constructions.

The authors introduce a domain-specific language for describing Euclidean geometry and use it to generate two datasets of concept-learning tasks. These tasks provide a shared setting for comparing human and machine generalization judgments. The emphasis is on recognizing what new examples share with a geometric concept, rather than merely recognizing familiar objects from natural photographs.

The study finds that humans generalize strongly from a small number of visual examples. In contrast, both low-level and high-level features from the examined standard vision models fail to support correct generalization. Geoclidean therefore exposes a specific gap between human geometric reasoning and the representations learned by those models. Its language and datasets provide a public benchmark for investigating that gap.
neurips-2022-geoclidean-few-shot-general.tldr: Geoclidean benchmarks geometric concept learning, revealing strong human few-shot generalization that the evaluated natural-image vision features do not support.

paragraphs: Graph few-shot learning asks a model to classify nodes using only a small number of labeled examples. Existing approaches often train across many classification tasks but compute node representations from the same original graph. As a result, a node can receive the same representation even when the set of classes being distinguished changes from task to task.

This paper proposes learning a separate graph structure for each task so that node representations can adapt to the current classification problem. The method extracts relevant nodes and uses node influence and mutual information to learn the task-specific structure. This changes the relationships used to represent a node, allowing the representation to reflect the task’s particular distinctions.

The authors evaluate the framework on five node-classification datasets, covering settings with one graph and with multiple graphs. They report improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. The findings support the idea that few-shot adaptation on graphs can benefit from changing the structure used for representation learning, rather than relying on a fixed graph representation across all tasks.
neurips-2022-graph-few-shot-learning-wit.tldr: Learning a graph structure for each few-shot task produces adaptive node representations and improves classification in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: This paper studies repeated games in which each player learns how to act over time. Regret measures the accumulated loss relative to the best fixed strategy in hindsight. Earlier work achieved very slowly growing regret for particular structured games; the authors extend logarithmic regret to games with concave utilities and arbitrary convex, compact strategy sets.

When all players use the proposed uncoupled learning dynamics, each obtains O(log T) regret after T rounds. The method builds on optimistic follow-the-regularized-leader in a transformed strategy space. A distinctive ingredient is a self-concordant regularizer that is not a barrier for the feasible region, allowing the authors to obtain the stated guarantees in this broader class of games.

Efficient implementation assumes access to a proximal oracle for the strategy set, yielding O(log log T) per-iteration complexity. The paper also gives extensions for access to only a linear optimization oracle. Separately, an adaptation guarantees O(sqrt(T)) regret in adversarial settings. These are different guarantees for different interaction conditions, with improvements over prior applicable results in iteration or dimension dependence.
neurips-2022-near-optimal-no-regret-lear.tldr: The paper establishes logarithmic per-player regret in general convex games when all players use its dynamics, with efficient updates under oracle assumptions.

paragraphs: Neural radiance fields reconstruct scenes from images so they can be rendered from new viewpoints. When the images are taken through glass, however, the reconstruction can include unwanted reflections along with the scene behind it. This paper targets the transmitted scene: the content visible through the glass that reflection interference makes harder to recover.

The proposed neural transmitted radiance field uses a transmission encoder together with recurring edge constraints to guide reconstruction. These additions are intended to help the model resist reflection interference when producing new views. The task therefore goes beyond reproducing everything visible in the input photographs; it seeks a representation that renders the desired scene despite contaminated observations.

The authors report high-fidelity reconstructions even when only sparse views are available. Experiments on a newly collected dataset show superior performance compared with state-of-the-art methods. The findings support incorporating transmission-oriented guidance into radiance-field reconstruction when the source images contain reflections, with the reported benefit covering both interference handling and reconstruction from limited viewpoints.
neurips-2022-neural-transmitted-radiance.tldr: Neural transmitted radiance fields use transmission guidance and recurring edges to reconstruct new views of scenes behind glass despite reflections.

paragraphs: Knowledge graph embeddings represent entities and relations numerically to help predict missing links. Images, text, and other modalities can enrich those representations, but their embedding spaces may have different structures. The paper argues that directly combining these spaces can disrupt the relationships already encoded within each modality, undermining the purpose of adding information.

OTKGE treats combination as a distribution-alignment problem. It constructs a transport plan that moves embeddings from different modalities into a shared space, minimizing the Wasserstein distance between their distributions. This makes the arrangement of representations part of the fusion objective, rather than treating multimodal integration as a direct combination of unrelated coordinates.

The authors provide a theoretical result guaranteeing consistency and comprehensiveness through minimizing the Wasserstein distances between individual modalities and the unified embedding space. They also report state-of-the-art performance on established multimodal knowledge graph completion benchmarks. Together, the theoretical and empirical contributions support optimal transport as a way to integrate heterogeneous information while retaining useful structure for predicting missing graph relationships.
neurips-2022-otkge-multi-modal-knowledge.tldr: OTKGE aligns multimodal embedding distributions through optimal transport to improve knowledge graph completion while preserving structured information.

paragraphs: Large recommender systems must retrieve a small number of useful items from enormous collections. A common approach learns user and item embeddings, then builds an approximate nearest-neighbor index separately. RecForest addresses the possible mismatch between those stages by learning the representations and retrieval index together, aiming for both efficient search and accurate recommendations.

The index contains multiple branching trees built through hierarchical balanced clustering of items. Within each tree, an item corresponds to a unique route from the root to a leaf. A routing network encodes user information and uses a Transformer decoder with beam search to identify promising items. Multiple trees help alleviate errors involving items near partition boundaries.

Parameters are shared across tree levels to reduce index memory requirements. The authors evaluate RecForest on five recommendation datasets and report better accuracy and efficiency than competitive baselines, along with substantially simplified training cost. The results support treating retrieval structure as part of the learning problem, so that the model’s representations and the routes used to access items develop together.
neurips-2022-recommender-forest-for-effi.tldr: RecForest jointly learns item representations and a multi-tree retrieval index, improving recommendation accuracy and efficiency in five dataset evaluations.

paragraphs: Adversarial training exposes a model to deliberately perturbed inputs to make its predictions harder to manipulate. This paper examines another property of the resulting models: how confident they are in their decisions. The motivation is to understand effects of robustness training beyond performance against attacks, including behavior on ordinary, unmodified images.

The authors empirically analyze a variety of adversarially trained models that achieve high robust accuracy against strong attacks. They find that these models are significantly less overconfident than non-robust models, even on clean data. This distinguishes the finding from the usual robustness result: the observed change concerns confidence in predictions as well as resistance to input manipulation.

The analysis also shows that architectural components, including activation functions and pooling, strongly influence prediction confidence. Thus the reported confidence behavior reflects more than the training procedure alone. The study provides empirical evidence connecting adversarial robustness and reduced overconfidence in the models examined, while also identifying model design as an important part of understanding that relationship.
neurips-2022-robust-models-are-less-over.tldr: The evaluated adversarially trained models are less overconfident even on clean images, with architecture also strongly influencing prediction confidence.

paragraphs: Sequential Monte Carlo approximates hidden-state distributions by sampling through a sequence of targets. Those targets commonly use filtering distributions, which incorporate observations only up to the current point. SIXO instead seeks targets resembling smoothing distributions, allowing later observations to inform inference about earlier hidden states.

The method learns functions that transform filtering targets toward smoothing targets through density-ratio estimation. Intuitively, the learned functions adjust how states are weighted so that the target reflects information from the full observation sequence. The authors then use Sequential Monte Carlo with these learned targets to construct a variational objective for learning both the model and its sampling proposals.

The paper establishes tighter lower bounds on the log marginal likelihood and reports more accurate posterior inference and parameter estimates across several domains. These contributions connect better use of observations with both inference and learning: changing the intermediate targets can improve the approximation of hidden states and the objective used to fit the underlying model.
neurips-2022-sixo-smoothing-inference-wi.tldr: SIXO learns smoothing-aware sampling targets that incorporate future observations, yielding tighter likelihood bounds and improved inference and parameter estimation.

paragraphs: Choosing a kernel is a central modeling decision for Gaussian processes and often requires expert input. Automating that choice can be expensive because evaluating model-selection criteria typically has cubic dependence on the number of samples. This paper develops a more efficient way to search a structured space of candidate kernels using Bayesian optimization.

The search itself needs a way to compare kernels, expressed as a kernel over candidate kernels. Previous approaches constructed this comparison by measuring distances between Gaussian processes in function space. The proposed approach instead compares symbolic representations of the statistical hypotheses associated with kernels. This shifts the search’s similarity measure toward the structure of the candidate model descriptions.

The authors empirically show that their approach makes searching a discrete kernel space more computationally efficient. The contribution concerns how the automated search organizes and compares possible models, rather than a claim that kernel choice no longer matters. It offers a structural alternative for guiding an expensive selection process toward useful candidates.
neurips-2022-structural-kernel-search-vi.tldr: Comparing symbolic kernel representations makes Bayesian optimization over discrete Gaussian-process kernel choices more computationally efficient in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Unsupervised skill discovery aims to learn varied behaviors without an externally supplied reward function. Many existing methods train several skills in parallel. This paper identifies a problem that can occur when the states visited by those skills overlap: parallel training can obstruct exploration, leaving the agent with limited state coverage and a less diverse collection of behaviors.

Recurrent Skill Training, or ReST, changes how learning is scheduled. It trains skills one after another and repeatedly returns to them, rather than updating all skills in parallel. This schedule is paired with an intrinsic reward based on state coverage. Together, the training order and internally generated reward are designed to address the exploration problem the authors observe.

Experiments cover challenging two-dimensional navigation tasks and robotic locomotion environments. ReST outperforms earlier parallel-training approaches on state coverage and skill diversity in these evaluations. The findings indicate that the organization of skill training can materially affect what behaviors are discovered, alongside the reward used to encourage exploration.
neurips-2022-unsupervised-skill-discover.tldr: ReST repeatedly trains skills in sequence with a state-coverage reward, improving exploration and skill diversity over parallel training in the evaluated environments.

paragraphs: Some offline reinforcement-learning methods learn to predict actions conditioned on a requested return. In a stochastic environment, however, a high-return trajectory may reflect fortunate events rather than reliably good decisions. Conditioning directly on that outcome can therefore suggest actions that do not deliver the requested performance on average.

ESPER addresses this problem by conditioning on learned average returns that are independent of environmental randomness. The intended distinction is between a result that happened once and performance that can be expected despite chance. This changes the conditioning signal while retaining the broader approach of learning behavior through a prediction task.

The authors evaluate ESPER on several stochastic offline-learning tasks, including 2048 and Connect Four against a stochastic opponent. In every tested domain, it aligns requested and achieved returns significantly better than direct return conditioning. It also achieves higher maximum performance than the evaluated value-based baselines. These findings support separating environmental luck from the target signal when learning policies from recorded trajectories.
neurips-2022-you-cant-count-on-luck-why-.tldr: ESPER conditions policies on learned average returns independent of environmental randomness, improving target-performance alignment in tested stochastic tasks.

paragraphs: This paper seeks to make vision-language pretraining with frozen large language models more effective. Such systems use visual features as prompts for a language model. The proposed approach focuses on the language side of that connection: learning which prompts are suitable for alignment with visual features.

The authors introduce a Prompt-Transformer, called P-Former, that predicts these prompts. It is trained entirely on linguistic data, so this additional stage does not require image-text pairs. The overall process gains a separate language-pretraining stage that can prepare prompt representations before they are used in vision-language learning.

Experiments show substantial improvements to the BLIP-2 image-to-text baseline and a reduced performance gap between systems trained with four million and 129 million image-text pairs. The authors also demonstrate the approach on a video-learning task using varied base modules, supporting its architectural flexibility and applicability across modalities. The findings suggest that language-only preparation can improve the use of paired visual-language training data.
neurips-2023-bootstrapping-vision-langua.tldr: A language-only Prompt-Transformer improves frozen-LLM vision-language learning and narrows the reported performance gap between smaller and much larger paired datasets.

paragraphs: Cross-Episodic Curriculum, or CEC, organizes experiences from multiple episodes inside a Transformer agent’s context. The aim is to improve learning efficiency and generalization by making progression across episodes available to the model. The curriculum is built from ordered experiences that show learning or increasing proficiency.

The method structures online learning trials and demonstrations of mixed quality into sequences. Cross-episodic attention can then operate over those sequences, allowing the Transformer to recognize patterns in how behavior improves. This places the development of expertise within the context supplied to the agent, rather than presenting each episode without that surrounding progression.

The authors demonstrate CEC in two settings: multitask reinforcement learning with discrete control in DeepMind Lab, and imitation learning with continuous control in RoboMimic. The first captures learning progression, including progressively complex settings; the second captures differences in demonstrator expertise. Across the evaluated instances, resulting policies show superior performance and strong generalization, supporting the usefulness of organizing context around improvement across episodes.
neurips-2023-cross-episodic-curriculum-f.tldr: CEC arranges experiences across episodes into curricula that help Transformer agents learn patterns of improvement and generalize in the evaluated control tasks.

paragraphs: SAMS-VAE models how interventions change cellular observations while seeking representations that are interpretable and composable. This is useful for studying perturbations whose biological mechanisms may be unknown. The model separates variation specific to an individual sample from shared effects associated with an intervention.

It represents a perturbed sample’s latent state as the sum of a local variable and global intervention-effect variables. Sparsity restricts each perturbation’s global effects to a subset of the latent representation. This is intended to identify distinct perturbation-specific subspaces that can be combined flexibly, linking the model’s internal organization to reasoning about multiple interventions.

The authors evaluate SAMS-VAE on two single-cell sequencing datasets and introduce an evaluation framework using average treatment effects with connections to posterior predictive checks. The model outperforms comparable approaches on evaluated in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks, including combinatorial reasoning with limited resources. Its interpretable latent structures also correlate strongly with known biological mechanisms. These results support its use as a scientific modeling tool without equating those correlations with newly established mechanisms.
neurips-2023-modelling-cellular-perturba.tldr: SAMS-VAE separates sample variation from sparse intervention effects, improving evaluated cellular-perturbation predictions while learning interpretable, composable latent structures.

paragraphs: PaintSeg segments objects by repeatedly modifying an image with existing generative models, without training a segmentation model. Its core process compares the original image with a painted version in which a masked region has been regenerated. Those contrasts guide refinement of the mask that separates the target object from its surroundings.

The procedure alternates two operations. Inpainting masks the foreground and fills the region with background, while outpainting masks the background and recovers missing portions of the foreground object. The authors describe this alternating process as gradually moving the segmentation mask toward the correct object boundary without supervision or additional training.

PaintSeg can accept several kinds of prompts, including coarse masks, boxes, scribbles, and points. The reported experiments show improvements over existing methods for coarse-mask, box, and point prompts. Its training-free claim concerns the segmentation procedure, which uses off-the-shelf generative models as a resource. The contribution demonstrates how repeated image generation and comparison can serve as a mechanism for object segmentation.
neurips-2023-paintseg-painting-pixels-fo.tldr: PaintSeg alternates generative inpainting and outpainting to refine prompted object masks without additional training.
